newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African trains troops for peacekeeping.
newsitem.headline: S.African trains troops for peacekeeping.

text.p: South Africa has trained two battalions to be ready for multinational peacekeeping and would be willing to contribute up to 1,000 men to any such operation, military officials said on Tuesday.
The officials made the remarks on the eve of a regional summit in Cape Town called by President Nelson Mandela to discuss crises in Angola, Zaire, Swaziland and Lesotho.

Mandela, chairman of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), will meet presidents Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe, Joachim Chissano of Mozambique, Ketumile Masire of Botswana and Yoweri Museveni of Uganda on Wednesday.

A South African foreign affairs spokesman said the meeting would follow up on contacts among the leaders over the last two weeks aimed at resolving, among other things, a national strike in Swaziland and a police mutiny in Lesotho.
The Lesotho army forcibly put down the police mutiny over the weekend but Swaziland is still tense.
South Africa, with one of the most modern defence forces on the continent, was asked last year to contribute to a multinational peacekeeping force for eastern Zaire.

The force was never fully deployed and South Africa balked at sending soldiers at the time because it said its new national defence force, comprising former enemies from the apartheid war, was not yet fully integrated.
However defence force officers told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday that two battalions were now ready for peacekeeping duties.
"The two battalions are trained and are ready to participate," army Colonel Jaco van As told the committee during discussion of proposed defence policy.
Members of the committee raised the possibility that South Africa, operating under the umbrella of SADC, could be called on to intervene militarily in Swaziland or Lesotho.
Brigadier Len le Roux, presenting the defence proposals to the parliamentary committee, said the army envisaged contributing mainly infantry to any peacekeeping force.

"The maximum scale that we foresee that it might be necessary to put in, would be at the level of an army battalion group, in the order of 1,000 soldiers supported by medical, engineering...and so on," he said.
"We don't see South Africa putting a division into this type of operation, I don't think we have the capability or the size."
Le Roux said that if South Africa was called on to contribute to a peacekeeping force, it would have one battalion ready to go with a second in training ready to rotate.
The defence force policy proposals said South African skills appropriate to peacekeeping included mine-clearing, communications and medical support.
